unit.sep: Classify carefully, trace supported transmission routes, use prevention evidence and separate actual observations from supplied records.
unit.careers: Illustrative public-health, food-safety and microbiology roles; no diagnosis or clinical treatment advice.
unit.focus: Microorganism groups, human infections and transmission, prevention/control, economic importance and daily-life effects.
unit.phenomenon: A fictional food-preservation message blames every microorganism for illness and claims a sealed picture proves which organism caused spoilage.
unit.supportingPhenomena: Teacher-reviewed infection examples, route-specific fictional cases, approved sealed observation or supplied dated records, and food-preservation evidence.
unit.drivingQuestion: What evidence helps explain how microorganisms affect people and how infection risks can be reduced? KICD: How are micro-organisms important in day-to-day life?
unit.storylineThread: Groups → beneficial/harmful roles → routes → infection types → matched prevention → control → economic role → preservation → safe inquiry → evidence limits → message → independent synthesis.
unit.content: Types of microorganisms; Mode of transmission and infections of different microorganisms; Prevention and control of microorganisms
unit.coreCompetencies:
Digital literacy: as the learner uses digital devices to research on infections caused by microorganisms as well as their control and prevention mechanisms.
Communication and collaboration: as the learner shares information gathered on types of microorganism infections, control and prevention.
unit.values: Respect is promoted as the learner becomes considerate of others’ opinion while discussing methods of controlling and preventing microorganism infections.
unit.pcis: Socio-economic issues (poverty eradication); as the learner sensitises the community on the significance of food preservation and the economic importance of microorganisms.
keyInquiryQuestions: How are micro-organisms important in day-to-day life?
unit.teacherConfirmationRequired: Teacher approval of public-health examples, any sealed sample, allergies and disposal; no learner opening/handling/sniffing/tasting of mould; actual digital/research/community actions recorded separately.

assessment.instructions: Independent written assessment,40minutes:5minutes read MI12,10minutes Section1,10minutes Section2,10minutes Section3,5minutes check. Use only the standalone final-only MI12 case and its printed source summaries. For each section cite the supporting source/fact and state an evidence limit. No access to teacher keys or teaching task cards. No diagnosis or unobserved performance claim.

sections.title: 1. Classify and explain a route
sections.prompt: Using MI12, identify the named microorganism group and infection category, explain the possible route, cite the supporting source and name one fact still needed before claiming what caused any real illness.
sections.exemplar: I1: V.cholerae=bacterium; cholera=bacterial; possible ingestion via contaminated water/food, supported by WHO summary; real exposure/contamination/cause still needs qualified investigation.

sections.title: 2. Match prevention and control
sections.prompt: For MI12 recommend two distinct general prevention/control measures matched to the water route. Explain a limit of EACH, cite the supporting supplied fact/source and identify when current public-health guidance is needed.
sections.exemplar: Use an authority-verified safe supply to reduce ingestion exposure; its verification and continuing safe handling are required. Use clean covered storage and utensils to reduce recontamination; this does not treat already contaminated water. These follow MI12/WHO water-safety reasoning; current authority instructions are needed for the suspect supply, and no actual cause is proven.

sections.title: 3. Explain a daily-life and economic effect
sections.prompt: Using MI12 and its CDC source summary, explain one possible economic effect of spoilage and select a preservation/storage approach suitable for the stated food and conditions. Explain why the evidence supports that choice, give one precise limit, and distinguish supplied business facts from measured local results.
sections.exemplar: Monitored refrigeration is supported for fresh cut melon by the supplied CDC summary and reliable refrigeration in the fictional case. Slower microbial growth may reduce unsaleable stock and replacement costs. Cooling does not sterilise or certify this batch safe; no exact savings can be calculated without quantities/prices. The vendor record is fictional, not measured local evidence.
